status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly praised the structural analysis as 'excellent' and agreed that 'the publication of the ECP6 structure will be a significant contribution to the field.' The crystal structure revealing intrachain LysM dimerization and the composite binding groove was not questioned, indicating reviewer acceptance of these structural findings.

Reviewers stated 'it is clear that the LysM1–3 binding site has sufficient affinity to work as the authors suggest,' explicitly affirming the picomolar affinity of the composite LysM1-LysM3 binding site. They accepted that this high-affinity binding explains how Ecp6 outcompetes plant receptors for chitin binding.

Reviewers did not challenge the ITC measurements showing micromolar affinity for LysM2 binding to chitin. They accepted these binding data as correct, stating 'assuming the ITC binding data are correct,' indicating implicit support for the measured affinities of LysM2 and its mutants.

Reviewers acknowledged that 'the LysM2 site can also work, apparently, in the absence of LysM1–3,' accepting the experimental observation that LysM2 suppresses chitin-triggered immunity. They did not dispute the alkalinization assay data showing this suppression, though they questioned the mechanism.

Reviewers raised a 'major concern' about how low-affinity LysM2 binding can suppress immunity, calculating that 'virtually none of it will be sequestered' at experimental concentrations. They stated 'the LysM2 domain does not directly out-compete for chitin-induced responses in the assay, and something else must be going on,' expressing uncertainty about the proposed mechanism while requesting stronger conclusions that LysM2 does not work via sequestration.

Reviewers noted that 'the data supporting this in the tomato alkalinization assay are not presented' for the T95R mutant from HEK293 cells, and that data was 'alluded to in the legend of Figure 6, but the figure itself does not show this.' They requested statistical analysis and clarification about whether L152R and S177K mutants show pH shifts, indicating uncertainty about the autoactivity claims.

Reviewers stated 'the authors state that the L152R and S177K mutants are not autoactive, but they do show some pH shift relative to Ecp6,' expressing uncertainty about whether these mutants truly retain full suppression ability. They requested statistical analysis to clarify this point.

Reviewers questioned the substrate-induced dimerization model, asking 'what is the evidence for this: why shouldn't the binding site be pre-formed in the protein?' This indicates uncertainty about whether the intrachain dimerization is truly substrate-induced or pre-formed.

Reviewers asked 'Do you actually know that the chitin oligomer bound to Ecp6 purified from Pichia is (GlcNAc)4? Could it be longer?' and suggested mass spectrometry confirmation. This indicates uncertainty about the precise identity and length of the co-purified chitin oligomer.

Reviewers noted discrepancies between current and previous work, stating 'in that paper, three binding events were documented; here it is two. What is the explanation for the difference?' They also requested control ITC traces and clarification about fitting of T22R and N47K data, indicating uncertainty about the ITC methodology and interpretation.

Reviewers did not question that HEK293-produced Ecp6 is chitin-free or that it can suppress immunity. They referenced this protein production method as a way to test specific hypotheses, implicitly accepting these claims about the HEK293-produced protein.
